did_you_know.text: Did you know? Tekhelet was an expensive blue dye in the ancient world, and producing it required special coloring materials. That made it a valuable and prestigious fabric.
Did you know? The biblical phrase “skilled work” describes artistic and complex weaving or embroidery, not simple sewing.
Did you know? We do not know exactly what the ephod looked like. The description suggests that it had sections worn over the shoulders and joined together.
Did you know? The biblical shoham stone cannot be identified with certainty today, so different translations suggest different modern names for it.
Did you know? A “zeret” was an ancient unit of length, roughly the distance from the tip of the thumb to the tip of the little finger, or about half a cubit.
Did you know? The names of the breastplate stones do not necessarily match the names of modern gemstones, because the meanings of the ancient names are not always certain.
Did you know? The twelve stones formed a complete representation of the twelve tribes of Israel, with a separate stone for each tribe.
Did you know? The Bible mentions the Urim and Thummim but does not explain exactly what they were or how they worked. Their nature therefore remains one of the chapter’s mysteries.
Did you know? The hem of the robe combined colorful decoration with sound, using pomegranates and gold bells arranged around it.
Did you know? This is one of the biblical passages in which sound serves a role in the proper order of worship, rather than being merely decorative.
Did you know? In the Bible, the word “tzitz” can also mean a flower or bud, but here it refers to a small gold plate worn on the forehead.
Did you know? According to this chapter, the high priest does not represent only himself; he also carries responsibility for the people’s sacred offerings.
Did you know? The phrase “fill their hands” is a biblical expression for appointing and consecrating someone to a role, not for literally filling a hand.

Did you know? Even within this elaborate ceremonial clothing, the Torah includes a practical garment meant to preserve modesty. The biblical word for these garments is related to the modern Hebrew word for trousers.
